extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents preparing or prosecuting patent applications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification and claims satisfy the written description, enablement, and definiteness requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA first and second paragraphs). Focuses on when to reject claims under 112(a) (written description/enablement/new matter) versus 112(b) (definiteness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctness of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) (or the first and second paragraphs of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112) are separate and distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a description or the enabling disclosure of a specification is not commensurate in scope with the subject matter encompassed by a claim, that fact alone does not render the claim imprecise or indefinite or otherwise not in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph); rather, the claim is based on an insufficient disclosure (35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA first paragraph) and should be rejected on that ground. (See opening paragraph and In re Borkowski, 422 F.2d 904, 164 USPQ 642 (CCPA 1970).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement must be commensurate in scope with the claims (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification's enabling disclosure must be commensurate in scope with the subject matter encompassed by the claim; the specification must teach how to make and use the full scope claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the disclosure is narrower than the claim scope, the claim is based on an insufficient disclosure and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Example: In re Mayhew — the only disclosed mode involved use of a cooling zone at a particular location; claims failing to specify the cooling step or location were held not to be supported by an enabling disclosure (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description/support for claimed subject matter (35 U.S.C. 112(a) first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims must be described in the application as filed; the specification must provide support for the claimed subject matter (written description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim (or an amended claim) recites subject matter that was not described in the application as filed, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as directed to subject matter not described in the specification as filed may be appropriate. Example: In re Simon — claims to a subcombination A+B+C were not described where the original application was directed to A+B+C+D+E, and the court concluded the subcombination claims were not described (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of critical or essential features may render claims unsupported
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification discloses that a particular feature or element is critical or essential to the practice of the invention, failure to recite or include that feature or element in the claims may provide a basis for rejection for lack of support or enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the specification indicates a feature is essential, claims omitting that feature can be rejected as not supported by an enabling disclosure. (Cited authority: In re Mayhew, 527 F.2d 1229, 188 USPQ 356 (CCPA 1976).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments that introduce subject matter not described in the application as filed (new matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims amended to include an invention or subject matter that was not described in the application as filed may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description/new matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an applicant amends claims to encompass subject matter not present in the original disclosure, examiners should consider a 35 U.S.C. 112(a) rejection. Example: In re Simon (reissue claims to a subcombination not described in the original disclosure). See also In re Panagrossi for related precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of disclosure (112(a)) should not be conflated with indefiniteness (112(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: An insufficient disclosure (specification not commensurate with claim scope or lacking necessary descriptive/enablement support) is a ground for rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a), not for a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness) rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner should frame rejections based on the proper statutory provision: lack of adequate disclosure/support -> 112(a); particularity/definiteness issues -> 112(b). The MPEP cites In re Borkowski to underscore that insufficient disclosure alone does not make a claim indefinite under 112(b) but warrants rejection under 112(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness / claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (35 U.S.C. 112(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement that claims 'particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention' under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph) is a separate requirement from the written description/enablement obligations of 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 112(b) is distinct from 112(a), an examiner should not substitute a 112(b) indefiniteness rejection for an appropriate 112(a) rejection when the problem is lack of descriptive or enabling support. The page emphasizes treating these requirements separately when evaluating claims.
